nodes.label: .claude/skills
nodes.why: Nine slash-commands that drive the vol project: compile and sync the guides, write a chapter, run a research sweep. The closest thing this repository has to an application.

nodes.label: hackathon/tests
nodes.why: The only automated test suite in the repository: 416 tests across ten modules, covering survey, resolve, render, runner, narrate, checkpoints and text handling. It imports the package by name, so it needs src/ on the path.

nodes.label: hackathon/tools
nodes.why: Four Node scripts that gate the artifact: self-containment, anchor and hash checks, fixture-chain consistency, and the splice that inlines a payload. No model runs here — this is the half of the project that checks.

nodes.label: guides
nodes.why: Three LaTeX guides, ~63k lines of .tex. The vol-learning guide alone is 371 pages across 22 chapters and is the repository’s main product.

nodes.label: hackathon/src
nodes.why: The generator package, and now the largest thing in the hackathon tree: all five stages plus the command runner, the quote resolver and the HTML template. Only narrate.py is allowed to reach a model.

nodes.label: hackathon/fixtures
nodes.why: Payloads standing in for pipeline output. Several fixtures describe one synthetic repo end to end, which is what check-fixtures.js exists to enforce.

nodes.label: reference
nodes.why: The paper corpus the guides cite: 98 tracked PDFs plus bibliography indexes. Papers arrive by hand or by the deep-research workflow.

nodes.label: notes
nodes.why: Append-only research findings. The vol-project rules make reading the journal step one of every session and appending to it the last.

nodes.label: hackathon/demo
nodes.why: The generated artifact itself: one self-contained HTML file carrying its payloads inline. The renderer of record now lives in src/trailhead/template.html and this is its output.

blocks.text: You need Node 22 and Python 3.11. One of the commands below fails on this machine and is shown failing — that is the repository’s current state, not a defect in this page.

stops.title: Five Things to Know About This Repository
stops.lede: Five statements, in the order a new joiner needs them: what this repository is responsible for, what flows through it, where its data comes from, what it touches outside itself, and where change concentrates.

claims.text: This repository owns the authoring and distribution of study and reference material for a Goldman Sachs internship on realized-volatility forecasting — planning, research and learning guides, not a forecasting system.
It is explicitly not responsible for shipping model code: its own working rules rank deep understanding of features and data above building fast.
Its main output is compiled PDFs pushed to a second branch: sync-docs recompiles the changed guides and updates docs-only with those PDFs, deliverables and notes.

Core data is a corpus of papers held as files, and one documented path brings new ones in — a research workflow that sweeps arXiv and SSRN and downloads open-access PDFs into reference/project-papers/.

The one interaction that reaches outside this machine is guarded in code: a pre-commit hook refuses any commit whose index still contains a .py file when the branch is docs-only, because that branch is cloned on a machine that flags code.

blocks.title: WHERE CHANGE CONCENTRATES
blocks.text: Churn and reach both point at the vol-learning guide: its chapters, main.pdf and references.bib hold the top commit counts, and one bibliography include serves all 22 chapters. That is analysis over git history rather than a fact on any single line, so it is marked inferred here and shown as measurements in the next stop.

blocks.title: ONE COMMAND IS MISSING FROM THIS PAGE
blocks.text: node tools/check-bundle.js was run and passed, but its output cannot be embedded here. The gate greps the whole file for stylesheet link tags and embedded font at-rules — and its own pass lines name both, so any artifact carrying its report fails it. The checker cannot tell real markup from string data inside the payload. Reported, not worked around: this sentence is written to avoid the tokens for the same reason.

stops.title: What green means here
stops.lede: Three gates, three different questions. Passing all three does not mean the pipeline works — it means the artifact is internally consistent.

claims.text: One gate proves self-containment by refusing any src, href, fetch or import that reaches a network origin, which is what lets the artifact open from file:// with the network off.
A second gate re-derives every anchor’s hash from the bundled excerpt, so a bundle whose source lines were edited after generation fails instead of rendering.
The gate scripts exit non-zero on any failure, which is what makes them usable as a build gate rather than a report.
Nothing runs these gates automatically — there is no continuous-integration workflow in this repository, so green is whatever the last person to type the command saw.

stops.title: Data Sources & Lineage
stops.lede: Code execution explains what runs. Data lineage explains where the values come from, how they change, and what they ultimately influence.

entities.name: The verified payload
entities.meaning: One verified.json per repository. It is the only interface between the generator and the artifact — everything this page shows is a projection of it.

steps.label: Fixture on disk
steps.description: A build manifest names one payload file per repository. There is no service call and no database — the payload is a file.

steps.label: JSON.parse
steps.description: The first thing the toolchain does with a payload is parse it, so a malformed file fails before any output is written.

steps.label: repo.name vs manifest key
steps.description: A mismatch between the payload’s own repo name and the key it is filed under is reported, not rejected — the build continues.

steps.label: Serialise into BUNDLES
steps.description: Each payload is written verbatim into a keyed map between two marker comments. Only that region of the bundle is replaced.

steps.label: loadRepo()
steps.description: The renderer selects one payload and binds it to D. Nothing below that point knows more than one repository exists.

steps.label: The walkthrough and its badge
steps.description: Every stop, the outline, the progress bar and the top-bar counts are rendered from the selected payload.

failure_mode.text: A payload named in the manifest but absent exits 2 before the bundle is touched, so a missing input cannot produce a half-written artifact.

boundary.text: Stage 4 (VERIFY) does not exist in this repository. The payload is produced outside it, so the lineage upstream of the fixture is not visible here.

tests.label: node tools/verify-contract.js fixtures/verified.ml-gs.json
tests.note: exits 0; re-checks every anchor in this payload

entities.name: Anchor excerpts and their hashes
entities.meaning: The evidence behind every factual sentence: the actual repository lines a claim cites, carried inside the artifact with a hash so the claim can be checked offline.

steps.label: Repository files on disk
steps.description: Each anchor names a path and a range; the lines are read from the working tree at generation time.

steps.label: files map in the payload
steps.description: Bundled as path → line number → text, sparse: only lines some anchor reaches are carried.

steps.label: anchor()
steps.description: Re-checks that the file is bundled, the range is inside it, focus lines fall within the range, no interior line is missing, and a hash is present at all.

steps.label: excerptOf()
steps.description: Rebuilds the hashed text: lines joined with a newline, no line numbers, no trailing newline. The digest is taken over exactly this.

steps.label: excerpt()
steps.description: Renders the line-numbered table behind each claim marker, highlights the focus lines and fills the COPY button.

steps.label: anchors sha256-verified
steps.description: The gate reports how many anchors re-hashed correctly. That count is the artifact’s claim to being checkable rather than merely asserted.

failure_mode.text: Editing one bundled line fails every anchor that cites it. Tampering with a single line of the sample payload failed both the claim and the trace hop sharing it, dropping verified anchors from 13 to 11 and exiting 1.

tests.label: node tools/verify-contract.js
tests.note: every anchor in every bundled payload is re-hashed

entities.name: Command capture records
entities.meaning: Proof that the setup and test instructions were actually run, including the ones that fail. Real exit codes are what separate this from a written guide.

steps.label: Commands run on the generation machine
steps.description: Each record carries the command, its exit code, wall-clock duration, captured output and an environment note.

steps.label: command blocks
steps.description: The captures enter the repository already as payload data; nothing in the tree executes them.

steps.label: the command case
steps.description: A non-zero exit must carry banner text, and every record must carry an environment note and non-empty output.

steps.label: none, deliberately
steps.description: Duration stays a display string and the environment stays a note. Nothing recomputes a timing, so nothing can quietly disagree with the run.

steps.label: B.command
steps.description: Renders the exit pill, the banner and the output. While a prediction is open the result is veiled rather than omitted.

steps.label: report.failed and the prediction key
steps.description: The failing-command count is cross-checked against the page, and the captured exit code is itself the answer key for the prediction above it.

failure_mode.text: A failing command with no banner, or any command with empty output, fails the gate outright — a broken setup step cannot be quietly downgraded.

boundary.text: No command runner exists in this repository. An external process produced these captures, but the runner cannot be identified from the available evidence.

entities.name: Python import edges
entities.meaning: Which module depends on which. This is what the architecture map is meant to be drawn from, and what checkpoint answer keys are meant to be derived from rather than authored.

steps.label: walk_files()
steps.description: Files are discovered under the resolved source roots and read from disk; this is where the repository enters the pipeline at all.

steps.label: extract_imports()
steps.description: Each file is parsed with the standard library ast and walked for import statements, producing one record per imported name.

steps.label: resolve_import()
steps.description: Prefixes are walked longest-first so a symbol import lands on the module that owns it; anything with no known prefix is external and is not a node.

steps.label: survey()
steps.description: The edges are assembled with the file tree, entry points and git churn into the survey payload that every later stage reads.

steps.label: mapper.order_nodes()
steps.description: Module-level nodes are ordered and packed into columns, so the graph’s geometry is decided at generation time rather than in the page.

steps.label: the module map
steps.description: What the reader sees on the map stop: node area from lines of code, edge thickness from the number of resolved imports.

failure_mode.text: A third-party import resolves to nothing and is deliberately excluded from the map rather than drawn as an unknown node.

blocks.title: HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE TRACE
blocks.text: The next track follows control flow — which function calls which. This one follows values: where each originates, what rewrites it, and which output it decides. Two entities below end without a consumer, which a call graph alone would not show you.

stops.title: How a payload becomes a page
stops.lede: The one end-to-end path that exists in code today: a JSON fixture becomes the data block of a self-contained HTML file, and is then re-checked from inside that file.

steps.claim: The fixture is read and parsed first, so a malformed payload fails before anything is written.
Each payload is serialised into a keyed map fenced by two marker comments, so only that region of the bundle is ever replaced.
The bundle is written back in place — which is also why this step is destructive on a file with uncommitted work.
Verification re-reads each anchor from the bundle, refuses one that carries no hash, and compares the recomputed digest against the recorded one.
Finally the report is cross-checked against the page itself: the ledger length must equal the reported drop count, and the number of failing commands must match.

stops.title: Checkpoint C
stops.lede: Put the build in the order the repository documents.

blocks.prompt: Order the four steps of regenerating the artifact after a payload change.
options: node tools/verify-contract.js — re-check every anchor and the report
Edit fixtures/verified.*.json — the single source of truth
node tools/check-bundle.js — confirm the file is still self-contained
node tools/inline-fixture.js — splice the payload into the bundle
blocks.provenance: The run order documented in hackathon/README.md and repeated as the change procedure in docs/verified-contract.md: edit the fixture, splice, then both gates.
blocks.explanation: Editing the HTML data block directly is the mistake this order prevents: the fixture is the source of truth and the splice overwrites whatever the bundle held.

stops.title: Where a change hurts
stops.lede: Four places where a small edit reaches much further than it looks.

claims.text: Changing how the excerpt is rebuilt — a different join, a kept trailing newline, line numbers left in — recomputes every hash and drops every anchor at once, with the payload and the source both untouched.
The checker rejects a block type it does not know, so a payload can only ship types the gate has been taught — but nothing checks the renderer learned them too.
A failing command must carry its banner text or the gate fails the bundle, which is what stops a broken setup step from being quietly downgraded to a warning.
An inferred claim carrying an anchor is rejected outright, because an anchor is what makes a sentence render as verified.

blocks.caption: Validation order, narrowest first. Commands are those documented in hackathon/README.md.
rows: Anchor, hash and report errors in the payload alone
Marker or brace-balance damage in the bundle
Broken inline JS, external loads, missing affordances
Fixtures that have drifted onto different repos

stops.lede: Everything in this stop is unverified. It is judgement drawn from the working rules and from what went wrong while this page was being generated.

blocks.title: THIS ENTIRE STOP IS UNVERIFIED
blocks.text: None of the statements below are anchored. They are the low-verifiability material, quarantined here rather than mixed into the anchored prose.

claims.text: Two sets of working rules apply in this repository depending on the directory, and they invert each other: the vol project is research-first and discourages jumping to code, while the hackathon rules ask for a rough end-to-end loop over any polished fragment.

The tree can change underneath you. While this page was being generated another session implemented all five pipeline stages, took the test suite from 8 to 416, and rewrote the demo bundle three times — falsifying several claims this generator had already verified.
Because most of hackathon/ is untracked, git will not save you from an in-place rewrite there — copy before you splice.
